subjects.name: Musik
subjects.description: Compulsory subject from Klasse 1 (typically 1–2 lessons a week), regulated only by Länder curricula — there are no KMK Bildungsstandards for Musik. In the Grundschule it is often taught by non-specialists; Länder programmes such as JeKits (NRW) and Bläser-/Streicherklassen in Kl. 5–6 add instrumental tuition.

subjects.name: Kunst
subjects.description: Compulsory subject from Klasse 1 (often 'Kunst' or 'Bildende Kunst'; in some Länder combined with Werken/Textiles Gestalten), regulated only by Länder curricula — no KMK Bildungsstandards. Recent plans (e.g. Berlin-Brandenburg 2017) are strongly process-oriented (Wahrnehmen – Gestalten – Reflektieren) and name few fixed contents.

subjects.name: Sport
subjects.description: Compulsory subject with usually three lessons a week, organised by Bewegungsfelder (movement fields) and pedagogical perspectives; regulated by the Länder (no KMK Bildungsstandards). Includes compulsory school swimming aimed at sicheres Schwimmen (Deutsches Schwimmabzeichen Bronze) by the end of the Grundschule and the annual Bundesjugendspiele.

subjects.name: Religion & Ethik
subjects.description: Religionsunterricht is an ordinary, confessionally bound subject (Art. 7 Abs. 3 GG — evangelisch, katholisch, increasingly islamisch, also jüdisch, alevitisch, orthodox); pupils who opt out attend an Ersatzfach — Ethik (e.g. Bayern from Kl. 1), Praktische Philosophie (NRW), Werte und Normen (Niedersachsen), LER (Brandenburg, ordinary subject Kl. 5–10); Berlin has compulsory Ethik in Kl. 7–10 with voluntary RU, Hamburg 'Religionsunterricht für alle'. This taxonomy covers the shared non-confessional core: knowledge about religions and worldviews, values and philosophical inquiry.

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Exploring Sounds and Silence
topics.description: Distinguish tones, sounds and noises (Töne, Klänge, Geräusche), experience and keep silence in listening games, and explore how sound is produced by striking, shaking, plucking, blowing and scraping — including with self-made sound makers (Klangerzeuger).
evidence: Sort a set of everyday sounds into tones, sounds and noises
Produce a sound on one object in at least three different ways (striking, shaking, plucking, blowing)
Stay silent in a listening game and name several sounds heard in the room
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you tap a glass, rustle paper and pluck a rubber band, can {{name}} tell you which one makes a clear tone and how each sound was made?

externalPrerequisites.subject: Sachunterricht
externalPrerequisites.reason: Listening games build on knowing how we hear

osMatches.note: os treats sound as physics (vibration); German topic is aesthetic sound exploration

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Keeping a Steady Beat
topics.description: Feel and keep the steady underlying beat (Puls) of a song or piece by clapping, walking or tapping, and tell the beat apart from the rhythm of the words.
evidence: Walk or clap in time with the beat of a familiar song for at least 30 seconds
Keep the beat steady while the music gets louder or softer
Show the difference between clapping the beat and clapping the rhythm of the words
topics.assessmentPrompt: When you sing a song like 'Alle meine Entchen' together, can {{name}} march or clap along steadily in time with the beat?

prerequisites.reason: Attentive listening to sound comes before feeling its regular pulse

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Echoing and Speaking Rhythms
topics.description: Echo and perform short rhythm patterns of long and short sounds with body percussion (klatschen, patschen, stampfen, schnipsen) and rhythmic speech rhymes (Sprechverse).
evidence: Clap back a four-beat rhythm pattern accurately after hearing it once
Perform a speech rhyme (Sprechvers) rhythmically with matching body percussion
Say which of two patterns has the long sounds and which the short ones
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you clap a short rhythm like 'ta ta ti-ti ta', can {{name}} clap it straight back to you accurately?

prerequisites.reason: Rhythm patterns are felt and placed against a steady beat

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: High and Low Pitch
topics.description: Hear and show whether notes are high or low and whether a melody goes up, down or stays the same, using hand signs, body movement and simple drawn lines.
evidence: Say which of two notes is higher
Show a melody's direction (up, down, same) with hand movements while listening
Draw a line that matches the up-and-down shape of a short melody
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you play two notes on a glockenspiel, can {{name}} tell you which one was higher, and show with their hand whether a tune goes up or down?

prerequisites.reason: Pitch is one property of the tones explored in sound play

osMatches.note: os: physics pattern pitch vs. object; German: musical pitch perception and melodic direction

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Loud and Soft, Fast and Slow
topics.nameDe: Dynamik und Tempo: laut – leise, schnell – langsam
topics.description: Recognise and perform contrasts in volume (Dynamik) and speed (Tempo), including getting gradually louder/softer or faster/slower, and use the first symbols p (piano) and f (forte).
evidence: Play or sing a passage loudly and then softly on a signal
Describe a piece as getting faster or slower, louder or softer
Match the symbols p and f to soft and loud playing
topics.assessmentPrompt: While listening to music, can {{name}} tell you when it becomes louder or softer, faster or slower — and play a drum 'piano' and 'forte' on request?

prerequisites.reason: Loud/soft contrasts are first met when exploring sounds
Tempo is the speed of the beat

osMatches.note: os: volume as vibration strength; German: musical dynamics and tempo

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Graphic Notation
topics.description: Represent sounds and musical events with invented or agreed graphic symbols (dots, lines, shapes), read such a score from left to right and play from it — the bridge to traditional notation.
evidence: Invent symbols for at least three different sounds and explain them
Play a short graphic score from left to right together with a group
Draw a graphic notation of a short sound sequence they heard
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a card with dots, long lines and zigzags, can they 'play' it on instruments from left to right and explain what each symbol means?

prerequisites.reason: Symbols stand for sounds the child can already distinguish
Graphic signs often encode loud/soft and long/short

externalPrerequisites.subject: Deutsch
externalPrerequisites.reason: Scores are read like text, from left to right

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Note Values and Rests
topics.description: Read and clap whole, half, quarter and eighth notes (Ganze, Halbe, Viertel, Achtel) and the matching rests, often with rhythm syllables (ta, ti-ti), and understand that each value lasts half as long as the previous one.
evidence: Name and draw whole, half, quarter and eighth notes and their rests
Clap a written rhythm of quarters, eighths and half notes in time
Explain that two eighth notes last as long as one quarter note
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a written rhythm with quarter notes, eighth notes and a rest, can they clap it correctly and stay silent on the rest?

prerequisites.reason: Note values notate the long and short sounds already performed by ear
Graphic notation prepares the idea that signs stand for durations

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.reason: Note values form a halving series

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Bars and Time Signatures
topics.description: Understand that beats are grouped into bars (Takte) separated by bar lines, hear and conduct 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 time and feel the stressed first beat (e.g. the 3/4 of a Walzer versus a march).
evidence: Count and conduct a simple pattern in 3/4 and in 4/4 time
Tell whether a piece heard swings in three or marches in two/four
Fill the bars of a given time signature correctly with note values
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you play a waltz and then a march, can {{name}} tell you which one goes in threes and count or conduct along?

prerequisites.reason: Bars group the steady beat
Filling bars requires knowing note values

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Reading Notes on the Staff
topics.description: Read the Stammtöne c'–c'' on the five-line staff (Notenlinien) with the treble clef (Violinschlüssel), on lines and in spaces, using the German note names c d e f g a h c — where German 'h' is English B.
evidence: Name the notes c' to c'' written on the staff, including the ledger-line c'
Draw a treble clef and place given notes correctly on lines or in spaces
Explain that the German note 'h' is called B in English
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a short melody written in the treble clef, can they name the notes — c, d, e, f, g, a, h — and show which one sits on a ledger line?

prerequisites.reason: Staff position represents high and low pitch
Reading melodies combines pitch and duration

externalPrerequisites.subject: Deutsch
externalPrerequisites.reason: German note names use letters of the alphabet

topics.laenderNotes: German note naming (h for B, b for B-flat) is used in all Länder; some schools introduce the staff already in Kl. 2.

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Scales, Half Steps and Accidentals
topics.description: Understand the major scale as a fixed pattern of whole and half steps (Ganz- und Halbtonschritte, e.g. e–f and h–c), and read sharps and flats (Kreuz, b) with German names such as fis, cis, b and es.
evidence: Locate the half steps of the C major scale on a keyboard picture
Name notes with sharps and flats using German names (fis, cis, es, b)
Build a major scale on G or F by applying the whole/half-step pattern
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a keyboard, can they show where the half steps are in C major and explain why G major needs an F sharp (fis)?

prerequisites.reason: Scales and accidentals extend the Stammtöne on the staff

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Singing Back a Melody
topics.description: Use the singing voice (not the speaking voice) to echo short melodies and song phrases in tune, with good posture and breathing.
evidence: Echo a short sung phrase at the same pitch
Switch between speaking voice and singing voice on request
Sing a simple call such as 'Ku-ckuck' matching the teacher's pitch
topics.assessmentPrompt: When you sing a short tune like 'Kuckuck, Kuckuck' to {{name}}, can they sing it back at the same pitch rather than speaking it?

prerequisites.reason: Matching pitch relies on hearing high and low

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Songs for Seasons and Festivals
topics.nameDe: Lieder im Jahreskreis: Kinder-, Volks- und Festlieder
topics.description: Build a repertoire of children’s songs, German folk songs (Volkslieder) and songs for the seasons and festivals of the school year — spring songs, Laternen- and Martinslieder, Advent and Christmas songs, birthday songs, songs from other cultures — and sing them by heart.
evidence: Sing at least five songs from the school year by heart, one of them with all verses
Name the season or occasion a song belongs to
Sing a lantern song or Christmas song with the class at a school celebration
topics.assessmentPrompt: When St. Martin or Christmas comes around, can {{name}} sing a few of the traditional songs by heart, like 'Ich geh mit meiner Laterne'?

prerequisites.reason: Learning songs by ear requires echoing melodies in tune

osMatches.note: festival songs as part of shared celebrations

topics.laenderNotes: Repertoire is chosen by schools; regional and dialect songs (e.g. Plattdeutsch, bairisch) feature in some Länder, and religious festival songs are handled with care in mixed-belief classes.

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Singing in Parts: Rounds and Two-Part Songs
topics.description: Hold one's own part while others sing something different — first in a round (Kanon, e.g. 'Bruder Jakob'), later in simple two-part songs and choir arrangements.
evidence: Keep their own line in a three-part round without drifting into another group
Sing an ostinato or second voice against a melody
Explain how a round works (same melody, staggered entries)
topics.assessmentPrompt: When the family sings 'Bruder Jakob' as a round, can {{name}} keep singing their own part while the others start at different times?

prerequisites.reason: A round can only be sung once the melody is secure
Staggered entries depend on a shared beat

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Playing Orff Instruments
topics.description: Name and play the classroom instruments of the Orff-Schulwerk — small percussion (Handtrommel, Klanghölzer, Triangel, Schellenkranz) and barred instruments (Glockenspiel, Xylophon, Metallophon) — with correct technique and care.
evidence: Name at least six Orff instruments and sort them by material (wood, metal, skin)
Hold mallets correctly and strike bars in the middle with a bounce
Play a simple rhythm or melody on a barred instrument in time with the group
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is handed a xylophone and a triangle, can they name them and play each the proper way so it rings out?

prerequisites.reason: Instrument technique builds on exploring how sounds are produced
Simple rhythms are the first things played

topics.laenderNotes: The Orff instrumentarium (Carl Orff, Gunild Keetman, 'Musik für Kinder') is standard equipment in German Grundschulen across Länder.

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Accompanying Songs with Ostinato and Drone
topics.description: Accompany a song with a repeated rhythmic or melodic pattern (Ostinato) or a drone fifth (Bordun, e.g. c–g) on percussion or barred instruments, keeping the tempo together with the singers.
evidence: Play a two-bar ostinato steadily through a whole song
Play a drone (e.g. c + g) on the beat on a barred instrument
Keep their accompaniment going when the singers move to the next verse
topics.assessmentPrompt: While others sing, can {{name}} keep playing a short repeated pattern on a drum or xylophone without speeding up or stopping?

prerequisites.reason: Accompaniment is played on Orff instruments
Ostinato and drone must stay locked to the beat
The child accompanies songs they know

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Playing the Recorder
topics.description: Play simple melodies on the soprano recorder (Sopranblockflöte) — starting with the left-hand notes h, a, g — with gentle breath and tonguing ('dü'), increasingly from staff notation.
evidence: Cover the holes correctly to play h, a and g with a clear tone
Tongue notes separately with 'dü' instead of blowing hard
Play a short song from staff notation using at least five notes
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has a recorder, can they play a simple tune like 'Hänschen klein' with a clean tone and no squeaks?

prerequisites.reason: Recorder tunes are usually read from the staff
Playing from notes needs note values

topics.laenderNotes: Not compulsory anywhere; offered as class instrument or AG in many Grundschulen. NRW funds JeKits (instruments, dance or singing, Kl. 1–4); many Kl. 5–6 offer Bläser-, Streicher- or Bandklassen instead.

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Class Ensemble Playing
topics.description: Play one’s own part reliably in a class ensemble (band, Bläserklasse, percussion group) from a part or play instructions, following conductor cues and performance markings (p, mf, f, crescendo, ritardando).
evidence: Play their part in a class arrangement from start to finish without stopping
Respond to conductor cues for entries, stops, dynamics and tempo changes
Explain markings such as mf, crescendo and ritardando in their part
topics.assessmentPrompt: In the school band or class ensemble, can {{name}} play their part all the way through, coming in on cue and following the loud/soft markings?

prerequisites.reason: Ensemble parts extend the accompaniment skills of the Grundschule
Parts are read and counted in bars
Ensemble playing relies on rehearsal routines

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Rehearsing and Performing Together
topics.description: Follow agreed rules in group music-making (start/stop signals, listening to others, careful handling of instruments), rehearse purposefully, present music to an audience and give appreciative feedback to others.
evidence: Start and stop exactly on the conductor's or teacher's signal
Take on a reliable role in a class performance (e.g. assembly or Schulfest)
Give a fair, appreciative comment on another group's performance
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}}'s class prepares a song for the school festival, do they stick to the agreed signals, practise their part and give kind feedback to others?

osMatches.note: group work transferred to ensemble music-making

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Mood and Effect of Music
topics.description: Describe the mood of a piece (cheerful, sad, scary, calm) and the musical features that create it, compare the effect of two pieces, and express what they hear in pictures or movement.
evidence: Choose fitting mood words for two contrasting pieces and give a musical reason
Paint or move in a way that matches the mood of a piece
Compare how two pieces make them feel and why
topics.assessmentPrompt: After hearing a short piece of music, can {{name}} tell you whether it sounds happy, sad or scary — and what in the music makes it sound that way?

prerequisites.reason: Mood is explained through loudness and tempo
Describing music starts with attentive listening

osMatches.note: emotion words applied to music

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Instrument Families and the Orchestra
topics.description: Recognise common instruments by sight and sound, group them into families (Streich-, Holzblas-, Blechblas-, Schlag- und Tasteninstrumente) by how they make sound, and know the groups and seating of the symphony orchestra as well as typical band instruments.
evidence: Identify at least six instruments by ear in a listening example
Sort instruments into families and explain how each family produces sound
Point out the instrument groups on an orchestra seating plan
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} hears a recording, can they pick out instruments like violin, flute, trumpet or timpani — and say which family each belongs to?

prerequisites.reason: Instrument families are defined by ways of producing sound
Hands-on instruments give a first reference for timbres

osMatches.note: instrument families are defined by how vibration is produced

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Musical Form: Repetition and Contrast
topics.description: Recognise repetition, variation and contrast as building principles of music: verse and chorus with intro and interlude in songs, and in Kl. 5–6 forms such as ABA and Rondo (ABACA), following them with form cards or movement.
evidence: Signal each return of the chorus (Refrain) while listening to a song
Lay out form cards (A, B) in the right order for an ABA piece
Identify a rondo by its recurring main theme and describe the contrasting episodes
topics.assessmentPrompt: While listening, can {{name}} raise a hand each time the main tune comes back and tell you whether the piece is built like A-B-A or A-B-A-C-A?

prerequisites.reason: Verse and chorus are first experienced in familiar songs
Form cards are a graphic representation

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Programme Music
topics.nameDe: Programmmusik (z. B. Peter und der Wolf, Karneval der Tiere)
topics.description: Understand that instrumental music can tell a story or paint a picture: follow how instruments and themes represent characters in Prokofiev's 'Peter und der Wolf' or animals in Saint-Saëns' 'Karneval der Tiere', and in Kl. 5–6 longer works such as Smetana's 'Die Moldau' or Mussorgsky's 'Bilder einer Ausstellung'.
evidence: Match the characters of 'Peter und der Wolf' to their instruments
Explain how a piece depicts an animal or scene through tempo, pitch and timbre
Retell or act out the story of a programme piece while it plays
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} listens to 'Peter und der Wolf', can they tell you which instrument plays the bird, the cat and the wolf — and why those instruments fit?

prerequisites.reason: Characters are identified by their instruments
Programme music relies on describing musical expression

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Opera, Ballet and Musical for Children
topics.description: Get to know music theatre — children's opera (e.g. Humperdinck's 'Hänsel und Gretel', children's versions of Mozart's 'Die Zauberflöte'), ballet (e.g. 'Der Nussknacker') and musicals — attend or stage a performance and understand the roles of singers, orchestra, dancers and conductor.
evidence: Explain the differences between opera, ballet and musical
Describe a scene from a children's opera or ballet and how the music supports it
Behave as an attentive audience member at a live performance
topics.assessmentPrompt: After a visit to a children's opera or ballet, can {{name}} explain what happened on stage and how the music, singing or dancing told the story?

prerequisites.reason: Following a staged story uses the link between music and mood
The orchestra is part of the performance

topics.laenderNotes: Live visits depend on local opera houses and Kinderoper/Jugendkonzert programmes, which are dense in Germany but unevenly spread between cities and rural areas.

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Creating a Sound Story
topics.description: Set a story or poem to sound (Klanggeschichte) by choosing voices, body sounds and instruments for characters and events, and perform it as a group with a narrator.
evidence: Choose a fitting sound for at least three events in a story and explain the choice
Play their sound at exactly the right moment while the story is read
Suggest a change that makes the sound story more exciting
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you read {{name}} a short story about a thunderstorm, can they choose and make sounds — with instruments, voice or body — that fit each part and play them at the right moment?

prerequisites.reason: Sound stories draw on the sounds the child can produce
Tension is created with loud/soft and fast/slow

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Improvising: Call and Response
topics.description: Improvise short musical phrases with voice, body or instruments, answer someone else's musical 'question' with an 'answer', and invent short sound sequences in group improvisation games.
evidence: Answer a four-beat clapped or played 'question' with their own four-beat 'answer'
Improvise a short sequence on two or three notes of a barred instrument
React to a partner's loud/soft or fast/slow impulse in a musical dialogue
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you drum a short 'question' to {{name}}, can they drum back their own 'answer' of the same length — something new rather than a copy?

prerequisites.reason: Answers are built from rhythm patterns
Melodic improvisation uses barred instruments

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Composing with Rhythm Building Blocks
topics.description: Compose a short piece by combining rhythm building blocks (Rhythmusbausteine) and simple melodic ideas, write it down in graphic or traditional notation, then rehearse and perform it with a group.
evidence: Combine at least four rhythm blocks into an 8-bar piece in 4/4 time
Notate their composition so another group can play it
Explain one choice they made to create repetition or contrast
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a set of rhythm cards, can they put together their own short piece, write it down and teach it to friends to play?

prerequisites.reason: Rhythm blocks are arranged in bars
Composing fixes ideas first found by improvising
Repetition and contrast structure the piece

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Moving and Dancing to Music
topics.nameDe: Sich zur Musik bewegen und tanzen
topics.description: Move freely and expressively to music, imitate and invent movements matching tempo, dynamics and form, and perform simple group and circle dances (Kreistänze, Volkstänze) from different cultures.
evidence: Change their movement when the music changes tempo or character
Perform a simple circle dance with the group, keeping the steps in time
Invent a movement sequence for the A and B sections of a piece
topics.assessmentPrompt: When music plays, can {{name}} move in a way that matches it — slow and smooth for gentle music, quick and bouncy for lively music — and join in a simple circle dance?

prerequisites.reason: Dance steps follow the beat
Movement quality mirrors dynamics and tempo

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Composers and Musical Eras
topics.nameDe: Komponistinnen und Komponisten, Epochen der Musikgeschichte
topics.description: Know lives and selected works of important composers — e.g. Johann Sebastian Bach, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, Ludwig van Beethoven, Clara Schumann — and in Kl. 5–6 place music in eras such as Baroque, Classical and Romantic.
evidence: Tell two facts about the life of a composer such as Mozart or Beethoven and name one of their works
Recognise a famous excerpt (e.g. 'Eine kleine Nachtmusik', 'Ode an die Freude')
Place three composers on a simple timeline of musical eras
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears 'Eine kleine Nachtmusik' or Beethoven's 'Ode an die Freude', can they tell you who wrote it and something about that composer's life?

prerequisites.reason: Works are recognised partly by their scoring
Listening to works builds on describing expression

externalPrerequisites.subject: Sachunterricht
externalPrerequisites.reason: Eras are placed on a timeline

topics.laenderNotes: The German-speaking canon (Bach, Händel, Mozart, Beethoven, Schumann) dominates; Beethoven's 'Ode an die Freude' doubles as the European anthem, and the Nationalhymne is a Kl. 5–6 topic (Hymnen).

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Music from Around the World
topics.description: Sing songs and dance dances from various countries and regions — including classmates' heritage cultures — get to know instruments of the world (e.g. djembe, darbuka, sitar) and compare occasions for making music in different cultures.
evidence: Sing a song in another language and say where it comes from
Name and describe two instruments from other parts of the world
Compare how music is used at a celebration in two different cultures
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} sing you a song in another language from school and tell you which country it comes from or which instrument is typical there?

prerequisites.reason: Songs of other cultures join the class repertoire
Dances of other cultures use the same movement skills

topics.subject: Musik
topics.name: Music, Media and Healthy Listening
topics.nameDe: Musik und Medien: Hörgewohnheiten, Lautstärke, Urheberrecht
topics.description: Reflect on where and how they hear music (radio, streaming, headphones), choose a volume that protects their hearing, and in Kl. 5–6 know the basics of copyright and personal rights when downloading, sharing or uploading music and videos.
evidence: Explain why loud music through headphones can damage hearing and set a safe volume
Describe their own and their family's listening habits
Explain why you may not freely upload someone else's song or a video of classmates
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} listens on headphones, do they keep the volume at a safe level — and can they explain why they shouldn't post someone else's song or a video of friends online without permission?

prerequisites.reason: Choosing a safe volume applies the concept of loudness

externalPrerequisites.subject: Sachunterricht
externalPrerequisites.concept: the ear and protecting the senses
externalPrerequisites.reason: Hearing damage is explained through the ear

osMatches.note: copyright/personal rights aspect only

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Mark-Making with Drawing Tools
topics.nameDe: Spuren legen und mit Zeichenwerkzeugen zeichnen
topics.description: Explore the marks that different drawing tools make — pencil, wax crayons, chalk, felt-tips, charcoal, tablet stylus — on different surfaces, and use them deliberately to draw people, animals and things from their own experience.
evidence: Produce at least four different kinds of line or mark with one tool (thick, thin, dotted, zigzag)
Choose a suitable tool for a task and explain the choice
Draw a scene from their own experience with recognisable figures and objects
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has pencils, wax crayons and chalk, can they show you the different marks each makes and choose one to draw something they experienced?

externalPrerequisites.subject: Deutsch
externalPrerequisites.reason: Controlled mark-making shares the fine-motor basis of handwriting

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Point, Line and Plane
topics.description: Use and name the basic elements of drawing — point, line, plane (Punkt, Linie, Fläche) — and line qualities (straight, curved, angular, thick, thin), inspired e.g. by Paul Klee's idea of 'taking a line for a walk' and Kandinsky's 'Punkt und Linie zu Fläche'.
evidence: Name and draw at least five different line types
Create a picture built only from points, lines and planes
Describe how Paul Klee used lines in one of his works
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you show {{name}} a picture by Paul Klee, can they point out the dots, lines and shapes and then make their own 'line walk' picture?

prerequisites.reason: Naming line qualities builds on varied mark-making

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Drawing from Observation
topics.description: Look closely and draw real objects, plants or animals from observation, capturing outline (Kontur), inner detail (Binnenzeichnung) and proportions — e.g. using Albrecht Dürer's 'Feldhase' as a model of precise nature study.
evidence: Draw a natural object (leaf, shell, flower) with recognisable contour and inner detail
Compare the drawing with the object and correct one proportion
Describe what makes Dürer's 'Feldhase' look so lifelike
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} draws a flower or a shoe while looking at it, does the drawing show the real outline and details rather than a 'standard' symbol?

prerequisites.reason: Observation drawing needs controlled use of drawing tools
Contour and inner lines are line types

externalPrerequisites.subject: Sachunterricht
externalPrerequisites.concept: observing and describing plants and animals
externalPrerequisites.reason: Nature study drawings accompany observation in Sachunterricht

osMatches.note: close observation, but in science rather than drawing

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Hatching and Shading
topics.description: Create light and dark tones and the impression of volume with hatching, cross-hatching and blending in pencil or ink, including cast shadows.
evidence: Produce a five-step tonal scale from light to dark by hatching
Shade a simple object (ball, cup) so it looks three-dimensional
Explain where the light comes from in their drawing
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} draws an apple, can they use hatching or shading so that it looks round, with a light side and a shadow side?

prerequisites.reason: Shading renders the light observed on real objects

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Portraits and Self-Portraits
topics.description: Draw or paint faces and self-portraits, moving from the early schema to observed proportions (eyes halfway down the head), and look at portraits by artists (e.g. Dürer’s self-portraits, Frida Kahlo) to see how they show personality.
evidence: Place eyes, nose and mouth in roughly correct proportion in a face
Use a mirror or photo to draw a self-portrait with individual features
Describe what a portrait reveals about the person shown
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} draws a self-portrait looking in a mirror, are the eyes placed about halfway down the head and does it show something individual about them?

prerequisites.reason: Portraits build on confident figure drawing

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Showing Near and Far in Pictures
topics.nameDe: Räumlichkeit im Bild: vorne – hinten, Überdeckung
topics.description: Move beyond the baseline (Standlinie) of early child drawings and show depth with overlapping, size differences, placement on the page (lower = nearer) and foreground, middle ground and background.
evidence: Draw a scene in which some objects overlap others to show what is in front
Make distant objects smaller and place them higher on the page
Identify foreground, middle ground and background in an artwork
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} draws a street or landscape, do they show near and far — e.g. houses in front overlapping trees behind and smaller hills in the distance?

prerequisites.reason: Spatial drawing extends early scene drawing

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: One-Point Perspective
topics.description: Construct simple one-point perspective drawings (Zentralperspektive) of a street, corridor or room with horizon line and vanishing point (Fluchtpunkt), and recognise perspective in Renaissance and later artworks.
evidence: Draw a horizon line and vanishing point and construct a box in one-point perspective
Draw a street or corridor whose lines converge in the vanishing point
Point out the vanishing point in a reproduction of an artwork
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} draws a long road or a corridor, can they use a vanishing point so the lines meet in the distance and it looks deep?

prerequisites.reason: Constructed perspective systematises the depth cues of overlapping and size

externalPrerequisites.subject: Mathematik
externalPrerequisites.concept: drawing straight lines and parallels with a ruler
externalPrerequisites.reason: Perspective construction needs accurate ruler work

osMatches.note: os uses parallel projections and explicitly excludes vanishing-point perspective; age 12-13

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Painting with a Paint Box
topics.description: Set up the workplace and use the school paint box (Deckfarbkasten with Deckweiß, on every German Grundschule supply list), brushes and water jar properly: wet the paint, mix in the lid, paint opaque or watery, rinse brushes and cover large areas without gaps.
evidence: Set up paint box, water jar, brushes and cloth before painting and clean up afterwards
Use a wide brush for large areas and a fine brush for details
Mix a colour in the lid and paint an area evenly and opaquely
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} paints with a paint box, do they wet the colours, mix in the lid, rinse the brush between colours and fill large areas without leaving white gaps?

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Primary and Secondary Colours
topics.description: Know the primary colours red, yellow and blue (Grundfarben) and that mixing two of them produces the secondary colours orange, green and violet (Mischfarben).
evidence: Name the three primary colours
Predict and then mix orange, green and violet from the primaries
Sort colours into primary and secondary colours
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} only has red, yellow and blue paint, can they tell you how to get green, orange and purple — and then mix them?

prerequisites.reason: Colour mixing is discovered while painting

osMatches.note: os: additive light/physics (age 11-12); German: subtractive pigment mixing (Kl. 1-2)

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Tints and Shades
topics.description: Lighten colours with white and darken them with black or a complementary colour, paint graded tone steps (Farbabstufungen) and use light–dark contrast deliberately.
evidence: Paint a scale of at least five steps from a pure colour to white
Darken a colour without making it muddy
Use light–dark contrast to make a figure stand out from its background
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} paint a row of boxes going from dark blue to very light blue by adding white step by step?

prerequisites.reason: Tinting and shading are further mixing operations
Graded steps need controlled mixing in the paint box

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Warm and Cool Colours
topics.description: Distinguish warm colours (yellow, orange, red) from cool colours (blue, green, violet), describe the moods and effects of colours and use them to express a feeling or atmosphere.
evidence: Sort colours into warm and cool
Paint the same motif once in warm and once in cool colours and describe the different moods
Explain the effect of colour in an artwork (e.g. Franz Marc's 'Blaues Pferd')
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wanted to paint a cosy summer evening and then a cold winter night, can they tell you which colours they would choose for each and why?

prerequisites.reason: Colour families are built from known colours

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: The Colour Wheel and Complementary Contrast
topics.description: Construct and read the 12-part colour wheel after Johannes Itten (Bauhaus teacher) — primaries, secondaries, tertiaries — find complementary colours (Komplementärfarben) opposite each other and use their strong contrast and other colour contrasts.
evidence: Paint a 12-part colour wheel with primaries, secondaries and tertiaries in the right order
Name the complementary colours of red, yellow and blue
Use a complementary contrast deliberately in their own picture and explain the effect
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a colour wheel, can they find the colour opposite red and explain why the two make each other 'glow' side by side?

prerequisites.reason: The wheel orders primaries and their mixtures
Tone steps are another colour contrast
Warm–cool is one of Itten’s contrasts

osMatches.note: physics of colour vs. Itten colour theory

topics.laenderNotes: Itten's 12-part wheel is the standard colour model in German Kunst textbooks for Kl. 5–6; some Grundschulen use a simpler 6-part wheel in Kl. 3–4.

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Cutting, Folding and Gluing
topics.description: Handle scissors safely and accurately, fold paper edge to edge, tear and glue, and use these skills to make paper objects (e.g. Faltschnitt, Fensterbild, a lantern for St. Martin).
evidence: Cut along a curved line with correctly held scissors
Fold a sheet exactly corner to corner and edge to edge
Assemble a simple paper object (e.g. a lantern or folded figure) from cut parts
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} cut along a wavy line and fold a sheet of paper neatly corner to corner, for example to make a paper lantern?

osMatches.note: os frames it as D&T making designed solutions (Science › Design & Technology)

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Modelling with Clay and Dough
topics.description: Explore malleable materials — modelling clay, salt dough, clay — by kneading, pinching, rolling and pressing, and form simple figures, animals and bowls whose parts hold together.
evidence: Roll a ball and a coil and use them to build a figure
Pinch a small bowl from a ball of clay
Join parts so that they stay together
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has a lump of clay or dough, can they model a small animal with body, head and legs that stay attached?

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Sculpture: Building Up and Carving Away
topics.nameDe: Plastik und Skulptur: Aufbauen und Abtragen
topics.description: Make three-dimensional works by adding material (additive: clay coil and slab technique, joining with slip/Schlicker) and by removing it (subtractive: carving soap, soapstone or aerated concrete with rasp and file), and compare both approaches.
evidence: Build a vessel or figure using coil or slab technique, joining parts with slip
Carve a simple form from soft stone or soap using rasp and file safely
Explain the difference between additive and subtractive sculpture
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain whether a clay figure and a carved soapstone were made by adding or by taking away material — and make a small piece in one of the two ways?

prerequisites.reason: Clay techniques extend free modelling

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Building, Constructing and Architecture
topics.description: Stack, connect and construct with boxes, sticks and found materials to build stable structures and models of houses, towers or imaginary cities, and look at architecture around them — e.g. Friedensreich Hundertwasser's colourful, curved buildings.
evidence: Build a free-standing tower or house model that stays stable
Use at least two different joining methods (gluing, slotting, tying)
Describe a special building (e.g. a Hundertwasser house) and what makes it different
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} builds a model house or tower from boxes and sticks, does it stand on its own — and can they explain how they joined the parts?

prerequisites.reason: Model building uses cutting and joining skills

osMatches.note: joining techniques; architecture viewing has no os counterpart

topics.laenderNotes: Hundertwasser (Austrian) is a Grundschule favourite in many Länder; several German schools and buildings bear his designs (e.g. Hundertwasserschule Wittenberg).

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Stamp and Material Printing
topics.description: Print with stamps (potato, cork, leaves, fingers) and later with self-made printing plates (foam, card, polystyrene), understanding relief printing: the raised parts print and the print comes out mirror-reversed.
evidence: Print a repeating pattern with a stamp, applying an even amount of paint
Make a printing plate from glued materials and pull several prints from it
Explain why letters or shapes appear mirror-reversed on the print
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} makes a print from a cut potato or a cardboard plate, can they explain why the picture comes out the other way round?

prerequisites.reason: Inking stamps uses the same paint handling

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Linocut
topics.description: Plan a black-and-white design, transfer it mirror-reversed to linoleum, cut it safely with lino tools (always away from the body, holding hand behind the blade), ink with a roller and print an edition — relating it to the woodcut tradition of Albrecht Dürer.
evidence: Plan a motif with clear black and white areas and transfer it mirror-reversed
Cut the plate with the holding hand behind the tool and the cut directed away from the body
Ink with a roller and pull at least three clean prints
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} makes a linocut at school, can they explain why the design is cut mirror-reversed and show how to hold the cutter safely?

prerequisites.reason: Linocut is a relief print with the same mirror principle
Black–white contrast is planned like tonal drawing

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Collage
topics.description: Collect, sort and select materials (papers, magazine pictures, textiles, found objects) and arrange and glue them into a new picture — e.g. inspired by Henri Matisse's paper cut-outs or Kurt Schwitters' Merz collages.
evidence: Collect and sort materials by colour, texture or theme
Try out different arrangements before gluing
Create a collage combining at least three different materials
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} gets a box of magazines, coloured paper and fabric scraps, can they choose and arrange pieces into a new picture with a clear idea?

prerequisites.reason: Collage relies on cutting, tearing and gluing

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Describing an Artwork
topics.description: Look carefully at an artwork, share first impressions and then describe it in a structured way — what is shown, colours, shapes, foreground and background, effect — using simple art vocabulary.
evidence: Describe what they see in a painting before giving an opinion
Use art words such as foreground, background, colour, line and shape
Link an observation in the picture to the effect it has on them
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you look at a painting together, can {{name}} describe what they see — what's in front, what's behind, which colours are used — before saying whether they like it?

prerequisites.reason: Describing pictures uses colour names and concepts
Own image-making sharpens looking at images

externalPrerequisites.subject: Deutsch
externalPrerequisites.reason: Picture description is a structured oral text type

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Interpreting and Judging Art
topics.description: Interpret artworks by connecting visual evidence (composition, colour, technique) with possible meanings and the artist's context, compare interpretations, and distinguish personal taste from a reasoned judgement.
evidence: Give an interpretation of an artwork supported by at least two visual details
Compare their interpretation with a classmate's and explain the difference in perspective
Distinguish 'I like it' from a judgement based on criteria
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} looks at a painting, can they suggest what it might mean, point to details that support that idea, and accept that others may see it differently?

prerequisites.reason: Interpretation rests on careful description

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Der Blaue Reiter: Franz Marc and Kandinsky
topics.nameDe: Der Blaue Reiter: Franz Marc und Wassily Kandinsky
topics.description: Get to know the Munich artists' group Der Blaue Reiter (1911): Franz Marc's animals in expressive, non-natural colours (e.g. 'Blaues Pferd') and Wassily Kandinsky's step into abstract painting — and create own works with expressive colour.
evidence: Explain why Franz Marc painted horses blue or yellow rather than brown
Tell a figurative painting from an abstract one
Create an animal picture in expressive, non-natural colours
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees Franz Marc's blue horse, can they explain why an artist might paint a horse blue — and paint their own animal in surprising colours?

prerequisites.reason: Expressive colour builds on knowing colour effects
Discussing the works needs description skills

topics.laenderNotes: Especially prominent in Bayern (Lenbachhaus Munich, Franz Marc Museum Kochel); Saxony and Berlin also feature the Dresden/Berlin Expressionist group Die Brücke.

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Art Across the Ages
topics.description: Place selected artworks on a timeline — cave paintings, ancient Egypt and Greece, medieval book illumination, Renaissance (Dürer), modern art — and recognise how the materials, purposes and styles of art changed.
evidence: Order five artworks from different eras on a timeline
Describe one feature typical of an era (e.g. gold backgrounds in medieval art, perspective in the Renaissance)
Explain why cave paintings or tomb paintings were made
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a cave painting, an Egyptian wall painting and a Dürer print, can they put them in time order and say something about why each was made?

prerequisites.reason: Comparing eras requires describing works

externalPrerequisites.subject: Geschichte
externalPrerequisites.reason: Art history uses the historical timeline introduced in Kl. 5–6

osMatches.note: art as historical evidence

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Visiting a Museum
topics.description: Visit museums, galleries and exhibitions as places where art is collected, preserved and shown; know museum rules, explore originals with looking tasks, and stage their own class exhibition.
evidence: Explain what museums do (collect, preserve, exhibit) and why touching is usually forbidden
Complete a looking task in front of an original artwork
Help plan and present a class exhibition with titles and labels
topics.assessmentPrompt: On a museum visit, can {{name}} explain why the paintings are behind ropes, find a favourite work and tell you something specific they noticed in it?

prerequisites.reason: Looking tasks in the museum use description skills

topics.laenderNotes: The Berlin-Brandenburg plan makes museums and other außerschulische Lernorte a mandatory part of the school curriculum.

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Taking Photographs
topics.description: Take photographs deliberately: choose the frame (Bildausschnitt: wide shot, close-up, detail), the viewpoint (worm's-eye, eye-level, bird's-eye) and light, and explain how these choices change the effect of a picture.
evidence: Photograph the same object as a close-up and as a wide shot
Take photos from a worm's-eye and a bird's-eye view and describe the different effects
Select the best of several photos and justify the choice
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} photographs a toy figure, can they make it look huge or tiny by changing the camera angle — and explain why?

prerequisites.reason: Framing and viewpoint relate to near/far in pictures

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Digital Image Editing
topics.description: Edit and combine images with a tablet or computer app (crop, adjust colour, layers, digital collage) and recognise that photos in media and advertising are often manipulated.
evidence: Crop and colour-adjust a photo to change its effect
Create a digital collage combining at least two images
Spot signs of manipulation in an edited image and explain why images are edited in advertising
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} edits a photo on a tablet, can they explain what they changed — and do they know that pictures in adverts or on social media are often edited too?

prerequisites.reason: Editing starts from own photographs
Digital collage transfers the collage principle

externalPrerequisites.subject: Informatik
externalPrerequisites.reason: Image editing requires basic device handling

osMatches.note: recognising manipulated images supports judging reliability

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Lettering and Poster Design
topics.description: Design letters and words decoratively (Schmuckschrift, calligraphy, tags), combine image and text on a poster or invitation that is readable from a distance, and analyse how posters and adverts attract attention.
evidence: Design a decorative initial or name lettering
Create a poster with headline, image and information arranged for readability from a distance
Explain how a real poster or advert uses colour, size and position to attract attention
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} designs a poster for the school festival, can people read the main information from across the room — and can they explain why they arranged it that way?

prerequisites.reason: Letter design uses line and plane
Poster colours are chosen for effect

externalPrerequisites.subject: Deutsch
externalPrerequisites.reason: Lettering builds on letter forms learned in Deutsch

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Stop-Motion Animation
topics.description: Plan a short stop-motion film with a storyboard, build figures and sets, shoot frame by frame on a tablet and understand how the illusion of movement arises from a sequence of still images (as in a flip book).
evidence: Make a flip book showing a smooth movement
Draw a storyboard of at least six frames for a short scene
Produce a short stop-motion clip with consistent framing
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain how a cartoon or stop-motion film makes things seem to move — and make a short flip book or animation themselves?

prerequisites.reason: Stop-motion is shot as a series of photographs
Figures are often modelled from clay

topics.subject: Kunst
topics.name: Bauhaus and Product Design
topics.nameDe: Bauhaus und Design: Form und Funktion
topics.description: Learn about the Bauhaus (Weimar 1919, Dessau, Berlin) and its idea that form follows function, with basic shapes and colours; analyse everyday objects as designed products and design a functional object of their own.
evidence: Identify the Bauhaus as a German school of art and design and name one typical feature
Analyse an everyday object in terms of form, function and material
Design a model of a functional object and justify the design decisions
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a simple Bauhaus lamp or chair, can they explain the idea 'form follows function' and design an everyday object of their own with that idea?

prerequisites.reason: Design models build on constructing
Itten’s colour theory comes from the Bauhaus

osMatches.note: design factors (function, appearance) without the Bauhaus art-history frame

topics.laenderNotes: The Bauhaus World Heritage sites lie in Thüringen (Weimar), Sachsen-Anhalt (Dessau) and Brandenburg (Bernau); the topic is emphasised especially there and in Berlin (Bauhaus-Archiv).

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Sprinting and Relays
topics.description: Run fast forwards on the balls of the feet with active arm swing, react to start signals from different starting positions, and run relays (Pendel-, Umkehrstaffel) with a clean hand-over.
evidence: Sprint 30–50 m on the balls of the feet with arms swinging opposite to the legs
React quickly to a start signal from standing, kneeling or lying positions
Hand over a baton or tag the next runner in a relay without stopping
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} races friends, do they run on the balls of their feet with arms swinging, react fast to 'Los!' and hand over smoothly in a relay?

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Endurance Running
topics.description: Run continuously at an even pace for a time linked to age — the Berlin-Brandenburg benchmarks are 'own age in minutes' (Kl. 1–2), age + 2 minutes (Kl. 3–4) and age + 5 minutes (Kl. 5–6) — choosing a sustainable tempo.
evidence: Run without walking for as many minutes as their age
Keep an even pace over several laps instead of sprinting off
In Kl. 5–6, run their age + 5 minutes and describe how they paced themselves
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is 9, can they jog without stopping for about 11 minutes at a steady pace, rather than sprinting off and then walking?

prerequisites.reason: Running technique is shared with sprinting

externalPrerequisites.subject: Sachunterricht
externalPrerequisites.reason: Understanding pacing connects to heart and lungs

osMatches.note: knowledge that exercise is healthy, not the running skill

topics.laenderNotes: From Kl. 5 the Berlin-Brandenburg plan requires endurance to be specifically trained and tested every half-year.

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Jumping and Long Jump
topics.description: Hop and jump one-footed (left and right) and two-footed over small obstacles, then jump for distance with a run-up: accelerating approach, one-footed take-off from a zone or board, safe two-footed landing in the sand pit.
evidence: Jump over a row of small obstacles one-footed (left and right) and two-footed
Take off one-footed from a take-off zone after a rhythmic run-up
Land on both feet in the sand pit without falling backwards
topics.assessmentPrompt: On sports day, can {{name}} run up, take off from one foot in the take-off zone and land on both feet in the sand?

prerequisites.reason: The run-up for jumping is a controlled sprint

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Target Throwing and Overarm Throw
topics.description: Throw various objects accurately at targets and, using the overarm throw (Schlagwurf) with the opposite foot forward and a whip-like arm action, throw small balls (e.g. 80 g Schlagball, 200 g Wurfball) for distance.
evidence: Hit a target from 5 m with a beanbag or ball in at least half of the attempts
Throw overarm with the opposite foot forward and the arm drawn back behind the head
Throw a small ball for distance after a three-step run-up
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} throws a ball as far as possible, do they step forward with the opposite foot and throw from over the shoulder rather than pushing from the chest?

prerequisites.reason: Throwing at targets grows out of basic ball handling

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Bundesjugendspiele
topics.description: Take part in the annual Bundesjugendspiele, a multi-event in athletics (alternatively swimming or gymnastics): sprint, jump, throw and endurance run. Since 2023/24 Grundschulen hold it as a 'Wettbewerb' ranked within the age group; from Kl. 5 the points-based 'Wettkampf' is usual. Certificates: Teilnahme-, Sieger- or Ehrenurkunde.
evidence: Complete all disciplines of the athletics multi-event (sprint, jump, throw, run)
Explain the three certificates (Teilnahme-, Sieger-, Ehrenurkunde)
Set a personal goal for one discipline and compare it with their result
topics.assessmentPrompt: After the Bundesjugendspiele, can {{name}} tell you which disciplines they did, which certificate they got and what they want to improve next year?

prerequisites.reason: Sprint is a core discipline
Jump is a core discipline
Throw is a core discipline
The athletics multi-event includes an endurance run

topics.laenderNotes: Compulsory every school year in Berlin-Brandenburg (RLP); Länder differ in how binding they are. The 2023/24 switch to the Wettbewerb form for Grundschule athletics and swimming was publicly contested; gymnastics may still be run as Wettkampf.

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Orienteering with a Simple Map
topics.description: Find their way at running pace through known terrain (school grounds, park) using a simplified map or site plan: orient (set) the map and find the control points (Posten) in order.
evidence: Set the map so that it matches the terrain
Find at least five control points in the right order using the map
Explain the route chosen between two control points
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} gets a simple map of the school grounds with marked checkpoints, can they turn the map the right way and run to each checkpoint in order?

prerequisites.reason: Orienteering is run over longer distances

externalPrerequisites.subject: Sachunterricht
externalPrerequisites.concept: reading simple maps and site plans
externalPrerequisites.reason: Orienteering applies map reading on the move

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Water Safety Rules
topics.description: Know and follow the bathing rules (Baderegeln, as promoted by DLRG and Wasserwacht) at an age-appropriate level — swim only where permitted and supervised, cool down before entering, leave the water in thunderstorms, never push others in or jump into unknown water, and get help when someone is in danger.
evidence: State at least five bathing rules and the reason for each
Explain what to do if someone else is in trouble in the water (call for help, throw something that floats)
Recognise unsafe places for swimming (e.g. weirs, unguarded lakes, thin ice)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Before a trip to the lake, can {{name}} tell you the important Baderegeln — like what to do in a thunderstorm and why never to jump into unknown water?

osMatches.note: os covers water safety among roads, strangers and internet
leave the water in thunderstorms

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Getting Used to Water
topics.description: Become confident in water: breathe out into the water, put face and head under, open the eyes underwater, float on front and back (Schweben, 'toter Mann'), glide after pushing off and play in shallow water.
evidence: Blow bubbles into the water and submerge the whole head
Float on front and back for several seconds without aids
Push off from the wall and glide in a stretched position
topics.assessmentPrompt: In the pool, will {{name}} put their face in the water, blow bubbles and float on their back for a few seconds without holding on?

prerequisites.reason: Safe behaviour in the pool area comes first

externalPrerequisites.subject: Sachunterricht
externalPrerequisites.reason: Buoyancy is experienced bodily in the water

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Seepferdchen Beginner's Badge
topics.description: Pass the beginner's swimming certificate 'Seepferdchen': jump in from the pool edge, swim 25 m in one stroke on front or back (breathing out into the water when on the front), retrieve an object from shoulder-deep water, and know the Baderegeln. A motivating first step — but not yet safe swimming.
evidence: Jump in from the pool edge and swim 25 m without aids or stopping
Retrieve an object from shoulder-deep water with the hands
Explain that the Seepferdchen does not yet mean 'safe swimmer'
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} jump into the pool from the edge and swim a full 25 m length on their own, then pick up a diving ring from shoulder-deep water?

prerequisites.reason: Swimming 25 m requires water confidence, gliding and breathing out
Knowledge of the Baderegeln is part of the test

topics.laenderNotes: Many children earn it before school in clubs or private courses; school swimming usually starts in Kl. 2 or 3 (Berlin: Kl. 3).

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Breaststroke and Swimming on the Back
topics.description: Learn a recognisable stroke in the prone position (usually breaststroke with whip kick, arm pull and breathing in rhythm, or front crawl) and in the supine position (elementary backstroke or back crawl), including changing body position while swimming without holding on.
evidence: Swim 25 m breaststroke with a symmetric whip kick and breathing in the stroke rhythm
Swim 25 m on the back with a regular leg action
Turn from front to back while swimming without touching the wall
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} swim a length of breaststroke with a proper frog kick and then roll onto their back and keep swimming without grabbing the edge?

prerequisites.reason: Stroke technique refines the beginner’s 25 m swim

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Bronze Badge: Safe Swimming
topics.description: Reach sicheres Schwimmen as defined by the Deutsche Prüfungsordnung Schwimmen: head-first jump and 15 minutes of swimming covering at least 200 m (150 m in one body position, 50 m in the other), diving about 2 m to retrieve an object, a tuck jump (Paketsprung) from the starting block or 1 m board, and the Baderegeln.
evidence: Swim at least 200 m within 15 minutes, changing between front and back without holding on
Dive about 2 m deep and bring up a small ring
Perform a tuck jump (Paketsprung) from the starting block or 1 m board
topics.assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} swim for 15 minutes in deep water without touching the edge — covering at least 200 m — then dive to the bottom at 2 m and fetch a ring?

prerequisites.reason: Bronze requires a recognisable stroke in both body positions
Bronze builds on the beginner level

topics.laenderNotes: Berlin targets this standard by the end of Kl. 3, Brandenburg by the end of Kl. 4 (shiftable to Kl. 5–6 if pool conditions are poor); most Länder aim for it by the end of the Grundschule, but DLRG surveys report many children leave primary school without it.

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Front Crawl and Underwater Swimming
topics.description: Extend water skills: front crawl with alternating arms and side breathing, a short distance at full speed, underwater swimming (Streckentauchen), jumps from 1 m and swimming continuously for longer — the building blocks of the Silver badge and of self-rescue.
evidence: Swim 25 m front crawl with side breathing
Swim 10 m underwater after pushing off from the wall
Swim continuously for their age + 5 minutes
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} swim a length of front crawl, turning the head to the side to breathe, and swim 10 m underwater?

prerequisites.reason: Advanced strokes and diving build on safe swimming

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Balancing
topics.description: Balance safely forwards, backwards and sideways on narrow and unstable equipment (upturned bench, beam, rope, wobble boards) and hold stands in different body positions, e.g. the standing scale (Standwaage).
evidence: Walk forwards and backwards along an upturned bench without stepping off
Hold a standing scale for 3 seconds
Present a short balancing sequence including a turn on the beam
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} walk backwards along the narrow side of an upturned gym bench without stepping off, and hold a balance on one leg for a few seconds?

prerequisites.reason: Apparatus work starts with safe set-up and behaviour

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Forward and Backward Roll
topics.description: Roll forwards with tucked chin and round back, then backwards (Rolle rückwärts), e.g. down an inclined mat, standing up without hands; vary rolls on and with equipment.
evidence: Do a forward roll with chin on chest and stand up without using the hands
Do a backward roll down an inclined mat and land on the feet
Link two rolls into a fluent sequence
topics.assessmentPrompt: On a soft mat, can {{name}} do a forward roll with chin tucked and come back up to standing without pushing off with the hands?

prerequisites.reason: Mats must be placed and used safely

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Climbing, Hanging and Swinging
topics.description: Climb, support the body and hang on apparatus (wall bars, ropes, rings, high bar, climbing wall), swing rhythmically with body tension, and master apparatus courses (Gerätelandschaften).
evidence: Climb up and down the wall bars or a climbing wall safely with three points of contact
Hang and travel hand over hand along a bar or ladder
Swing on the rings with body tension and dismount safely
topics.assessmentPrompt: On the playground or in the gym, can {{name}} climb up and down safely, hang from a bar and move along it hand over hand?

prerequisites.reason: Climbing stations require safe set-up and rules

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Jumping, Landing and Vaulting
topics.description: Land controlled and with body tension after jumps from various heights (box, mini-trampoline), and later jump with run-up and springboard onto and over obstacles such as a vaulting box or buck (Aufhocken, Hocke, Grätsche).
evidence: Land from a jump off a box on both feet with bent knees, without falling
Jump onto a box after a run-up and two-footed take-off from the springboard
Vault over a box or buck (e.g. squat vault) with a safe landing
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} jumps off something high, do they land softly on both feet with bent knees — and can they jump onto a box after a run-up and take-off from the springboard?

prerequisites.reason: Jumping stations need mats and spotting
Take-off and landing patterns are shared with athletics jumps

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Handstand and Cartwheel
topics.description: Support the body upside down with straight arms and body tension: handstand against the wall or with a spotter, cartwheel (Rad) along a line, and other inverted movements (Überschlagbewegungen).
evidence: Hold a handstand against the wall with straight arms and a tight body for 3 seconds
Perform a cartwheel along a line with hands and feet placed one after another
Kick up into a handstand with a partner spotting and come down safely
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} do a cartwheel along a straight line, or kick up into a handstand against a wall and hold it with straight arms?

prerequisites.reason: Inverted movements build on rolling and body tension
Supporting the body weight on the arms is practised at apparatus

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Gymnastics Routine
topics.description: Combine elements from the different element groups (rolling, balancing, jumping, supporting, swinging) into a fluent routine on the floor or apparatus, present it with body tension, and design one with guidance.
evidence: Perform a given sequence of at least four elements fluently
Design their own short floor routine with clear start and end positions
Give a partner feedback on fluency and body tension using agreed criteria
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} put together and show a short floor routine — for example a roll, a balance, a jump and a cartwheel — that flows from one element into the next?

prerequisites.reason: Rolls are core routine elements
Balances are core routine elements
Inverted elements raise the routine level

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Tag and Running Games
topics.description: Play traditional running and tag games (e.g. 'Fischer, Fischer, wie tief ist das Wasser?', 'Feuer, Wasser, Blitz', Kettenfangen): grasp the game idea, take on roles (catcher, runner) and react to others' movements.
evidence: Explain the rules of a tag game and follow them
Switch roles (catcher/runner) when the rules require it
Dodge a catcher by changing direction quickly
topics.assessmentPrompt: When children play 'Fischer, Fischer, wie tief ist das Wasser?', does {{name}} understand the rules, swap roles when caught and dodge the catcher by changing direction?

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Throwing, Catching and Bouncing a Ball
topics.description: Develop ball skills with balls of different sizes: throw and catch with a partner, bounce (prellen) with one hand while moving, roll and stop a ball, and dribble with the foot.
evidence: Throw and catch a ball with a partner 3 m away ten times in a row
Bounce a ball with one hand while walking around cones
Dribble a ball with the foot around obstacles and stop it
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} play catch with you ten times in a row without dropping the ball, and bounce a ball while walking around the garden?

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Inventing and Changing Games
topics.description: Understand the elements of a game (rules, field, object, teams, roles) and change them deliberately to make a game fairer, easier or more exciting, agreeing new rules together.
evidence: Name the elements of a game they know (rules, field, object, teams, roles)
Change one element of a game and explain the effect
Agree a rule change with the group and play the new version fairly
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a game isn't fun because one team always wins, can {{name}} suggest a rule change — like a smaller field or an extra player — that makes it fairer?

prerequisites.reason: Changing games presupposes playing and understanding simple games
Rule changes are judged by fairness

osMatches.note: making/changing rules, but in school community not games

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Völkerball and Brennball
topics.description: Play the German school classics Völkerball (a team throwing and dodging game with outfield and 'König') and Brennball (a batting/running game in which runners must reach a base before the ball reaches the 'Brennmal'), applying throwing, catching and running skills with team tactics.
evidence: Explain the rules of Völkerball or Brennball and when a player is out or 'verbrannt'
Catch or dodge throws and pass to teammates in Völkerball
Decide when to run and when to stay at a base in Brennball
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} plays Völkerball or Brennball at school, can they explain the rules and choose sensibly when to throw, dodge or run?

prerequisites.reason: Both games depend on throwing and catching
Dodging and running to safety come from tag games

topics.laenderNotes: Völkerball is debated among sports educators as a game that targets people; many schools use soft balls or replace it with Brennball or Ball über die Schnur.

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Team Games: Passing, Space and Scoring
topics.description: Apply core elements of invasion games (Fußball, Handball, Basketball) in small-sided games: receive and pass, carry or dribble the ball, find and use free space, offer for a pass, defend and finish on goal, using simple fakes (Finten).
evidence: Pass and receive the ball within the rules in a 3-v-3 game
Move into free space to offer for a pass
Score from movement after a dribble or pass, using a simple fake
topics.assessmentPrompt: In a small game of football or handball, does {{name}} move into free space to get the ball, pass to teammates and try to score — rather than everyone chasing the ball in a cluster?

prerequisites.reason: Passing and dribbling require ball control
Small-sided games use adapted rules
Team tactics are first met in simple team games

topics.laenderNotes: Which big game is taught (Fußball, Handball, Basketball, Hockey…) is left to schools; many Länder require Sportspiele mainly from Kl. 5.

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Net and Racket Games
topics.nameDe: Rückschlagspiele (Ball über die Schnur, Badminton, Tischtennis)
topics.description: Play return games over a net or line: from 'Ball über die Schnur' with throwing and catching to hitting a shuttlecock or ball with a racket (Badminton, Tischtennis) and volleyball-like volleys — keeping a rally going and placing the ball.
evidence: Keep a rally of at least five hits going with a partner
Hit forehand and backhand with a racket
Place the ball or shuttle into free space on the opponent's side
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} keep a badminton or table-tennis rally going with you for five hits, and sometimes aim it where you can't reach it?

prerequisites.reason: Return games require tracking and catching a ball

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Expressive Movement and Moving to a Rhythm
topics.nameDe: Darstellen und sich im Rhythmus bewegen
topics.description: Imitate and improvise movements (animals, machines, feelings) and move appropriately to a rhythm given by a drum, clapping or music, changing tempo and quality of movement.
evidence: Imitate an animal or object with whole-body movement that others can recognise
Walk, hop or gallop in time to a drum beat and freeze on the stop signal
Change movement quality (heavy/light, fast/slow) as the rhythm changes
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you beat a drum, can {{name}} walk, hop or gallop in time with it — and switch to slow, heavy 'elephant steps' when you slow down?

prerequisites.reason: Moving in time needs a felt steady beat

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Rope Skipping and Hand Apparatus
topics.nameDe: Bewegen mit Handgeräten: Seil, Reifen, Ball, Band
topics.description: Move objects in a controlled way according to their properties — skip with a rope (forwards, backwards, long turning rope), spin and roll hoops, swing ribbons, juggle scarves — and perform a short sequence with an object.
evidence: Skip with a rope at least 20 times in a row
Run into a long turning rope (Schwungseil) and jump in rhythm
Perform a short sequence with a hoop or ball to music
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} skip with a jump rope 20 times in a row without tripping, and jump into a long rope that others are turning?

prerequisites.reason: Rope skipping needs rhythmic jumping

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Dance and Choreography
topics.description: Perform and later design dance sequences in a group to music — children's and folk dances, pop and contemporary dance, juggling or acrobatics shows — counting in eights, starting together and presenting to an audience.
evidence: Perform a learned group dance in time with the music, counting in eights
Create a short sequence of eight-counts with a partner or group
Present a sequence to the class and accept feedback
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} learn a short dance with friends, count the beats ('5, 6, 7, 8') to start together and perform it all the way through?

prerequisites.reason: Dance sequences build on moving to a rhythm
Group dances are also learned in Musik
Counting in eights relies on feeling bars

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Scooter Boards, Scooters and Inline Skates
topics.nameDe: Rollen und Gleiten: Rollbrett, Roller, Inliner
topics.description: Move on rolling devices (Rollbrett, Pedalo, scooter, later inline skates or skateboard): keep balance in motion, steer around obstacles, brake and stop safely, wearing protective gear.
evidence: Ride a scooter board or scooter around cones and stop on a signal
Brake safely on inline skates (e.g. heel brake or T-stop)
Name and put on the right protective gear (helmet, wrist, knee and elbow pads)
topics.assessmentPrompt: On a scooter or inline skates, can {{name}} steer around obstacles and stop safely when needed — and do they put on helmet and pads without being reminded?

prerequisites.reason: Dynamic balance builds on balancing
Protective gear and safe behaviour are prerequisites

topics.laenderNotes: Winter sports (Skilanglauf, Eislaufen) and boating are offered under this Bewegungsfeld in some southern and lakeside regions.

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Bike Handling Skills
topics.description: Control a bicycle safely: start off, ride slowly and in a straight line, look back over the shoulder, signal with one arm, steer through a slalom and brake to a stop at a line — the motor basis for the Radfahrausbildung in Kl. 3/4.
evidence: Ride slowly along a narrow lane without putting a foot down
Look over the shoulder and signal with one arm while holding the line
Brake to a controlled stop at a marked line
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} ride their bike slowly through a course of cones, look back over their shoulder without wobbling and stop exactly at a line?

prerequisites.reason: Balance and braking on rolling devices transfer to the bike

osMatches.note: road-safety knowledge only; bike handling has no os counterpart

topics.laenderNotes: The Radfahrausbildung with the police-supported 'Fahrradprüfung' (usually Kl. 4) belongs to Sachunterricht/Verkehrserziehung in all Länder; Sport provides the motor basis.

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Play-Fighting by the Rules
topics.description: Wrestle playfully for objects, positions and space (kneeling or standing) while protecting the partner: fall safely from kneeling and standing, respect the stop rule ('Stopp!' ends the fight at once), no hitting and no painful grips.
evidence: Stop immediately when the partner says 'Stopp' or taps
Fall backwards and sideways safely from kneeling and standing
Win or defend an object or area in a ground-wrestling game using only allowed techniques
topics.assessmentPrompt: In a wrestling game, does {{name}} stop at once when their partner calls 'Stopp', and can they fall safely backwards without banging their head?

prerequisites.reason: Play-fighting is only possible with strict rules and respect
Safe falling uses the rounded back of the roll

osMatches.note: the 'Stopp' rule applies accepting 'no' to physical contact

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Partner Wrestling and Judo Basics
topics.nameDe: Zweikampf: Gleichgewicht stören und Festhalten (Judo, Ringen)
topics.description: Use strength and simple techniques purposefully to unbalance a partner and hold them down (Haltegriff), break-fall safely after a partner’s action, and solve wrestling tasks together — as an introduction to Judo or Ringen.
evidence: Break-fall correctly after being unbalanced by a partner
Apply a simple hold-down and keep control for 10 seconds
Explain and follow the safety rules and rituals of a judo lesson (bowing, stop signals)
topics.assessmentPrompt: In a judo or wrestling lesson, can {{name}} unbalance a partner using technique rather than force, and land safely when they themselves are thrown?

prerequisites.reason: Technique-based combat builds on safe falling and stop rules

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Fair Play
topics.description: Play fairly: keep to rules and agreements, admit fouls, respect opponents and referees, help others, and deal with winning and losing graciously (e.g. shaking hands after a game).
evidence: Follow agreed rules even when no one is watching
Admit their own foul or that the ball was out
Congratulate the winners or console the losers after a game
topics.assessmentPrompt: After losing a game, does {{name}} shake hands with the other team — and do they own up when they've broken a rule even if nobody noticed?

osMatches.note: following rules willingly; os not sport-specific

topics.subject: Sport
topics.name: Safe Set-Up and Spotting
topics.description: Follow safety rules in sport (sportswear, no jewellery, listen to signals), set up and dismantle apparatus correctly in teams (carry mats together, secure benches) and, later, give simple help and spotting (Hilfestellung) to partners.
